title: Cardiovascular II: Coronary Disease and Heart Failure
summary: Atherosclerosis, heart attacks and the failing heart.

lessons.title: Atherosclerosis

levels.kid:
Arteries are tubes that carry blood from your heart to your body. When they are young and healthy, they are smooth and stretchy inside, like a new garden hose.

Over many years, fat and other gunk can stick to the inside walls. This builds up into a lump called a plaque. The plaque makes the tube narrower, so less blood can get through. This is called atherosclerosis.

Sometimes a plaque cracks open. Then the body tries to fix it by making a clot, like a scab. But inside a tube, that scab can block the blood completely. Eating healthy food, moving your body, and not smoking help keep arteries clean.
levels.hs:
**Atherosclerosis** is the buildup of fatty plaques in the walls of medium and large arteries. It is the main cause of heart attacks, many strokes, and leg artery disease.

How it develops:
- The inner lining of the artery (the **endothelium**) is damaged by things like high blood pressure, smoking, high blood sugar, and high LDL cholesterol.
- **LDL** particles slip into the artery wall and become oxidized.
- White blood cells called **monocytes** enter, turn into macrophages, and swallow the fat, becoming **foam cells**. These form **fatty streaks**, which can be seen even in teenagers.
- Smooth muscle cells move in and build a **fibrous cap** over a fatty core, forming a mature plaque.

A plaque can cause trouble in two ways. It can slowly narrow the artery, causing symptoms when the body needs more blood, such as chest pain on exertion. Or it can **rupture**, exposing its contents to blood and triggering a clot that suddenly blocks the artery.

Major risk factors: high LDL, high blood pressure, smoking, diabetes, family history of early heart disease, older age, male sex, obesity, and inactivity. Many of these can be changed.
levels.college:
Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease of the arterial intima driven by retention of apolipoprotein B–containing lipoproteins (LDL, VLDL remnants, lipoprotein(a)).

Sequence:
- **Endothelial dysfunction:** reduced nitric oxide bioavailability, increased permeability, and expression of adhesion molecules (VCAM-1, ICAM-1, selectins), especially at branch points with low or oscillatory shear stress.
- **Lipoprotein retention and modification:** apoB particles bind intimal proteoglycans and are oxidized; oxidized LDL is taken up through scavenger receptors (CD36, SR-A), which are not downregulated by cholesterol, so macrophages become foam cells.
- **Inflammation:** cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α), the NLRP3 inflammasome, and T cells sustain the lesion.
- **Fibrous cap formation:** smooth muscle cells migrate from the media and produce collagen.
- **Necrotic core:** apoptotic foam cells that are poorly cleared (defective efferocytosis) form a lipid-rich, thrombogenic core with cholesterol crystals and tissue factor.

The **vulnerable plaque** has a thin fibrous cap (classically under about 65 µm), a large necrotic core, heavy macrophage infiltration, and positive remodeling. Matrix metalloproteinases from macrophages weaken the cap. Rupture exposes tissue factor and collagen, causing platelet adhesion and thrombosis. Plaque **erosion**, loss of endothelium over a fibrous, lipid-poor plaque, accounts for a substantial share of coronary thrombosis, especially in younger patients and women.

Importantly, many plaques that rupture are not the most stenotic ones. Because of outward (positive) remodeling, a plaque can be large while the lumen looks only mildly narrowed on angiography.

LDL lowering reduces events in proportion to the absolute reduction achieved. Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, upregulating hepatic LDL receptors; ezetimibe and PCSK9 inhibitors add further lowering.
levels.phd:
The causal role of LDL is supported by convergent evidence: Mendelian randomization of variants in LDLR, PCSK9, HMGCR and NPC1L1 shows that lifelong lower LDL produces proportionally lower coronary risk, and familial hypercholesterolemia produces premature disease. The cumulative exposure model (concentration × years) explains why early-life lowering has outsized effects. Lipoprotein(a), whose apo(a) component resembles plasminogen and carries oxidized phospholipids, is a genetically determined, independent causal risk factor; specific lowering therapies are under investigation in outcome trials.

Inflammation is a separate axis. The CANTOS trial showed that IL-1β neutralization reduced cardiovascular events without lowering LDL, and colchicine trials (COLCOT, LoDoCo2) supported anti-inflammatory benefit, establishing residual inflammatory risk as a target, with a trade-off of infection risk in CANTOS.

Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP), somatic mutations in TET2, DNMT3A and others in blood stem cells, increases atherosclerotic risk partly through enhanced macrophage inflammasome activity, linking aging biology to vascular disease.

Plaque biology also includes intraplaque hemorrhage from leaky neovessels, spotty microcalcification that concentrates mechanical stress in the cap, and smooth muscle cell plasticity: lineage tracing in mice shows many cells in plaques that express macrophage markers are actually of smooth muscle origin, revising the classic foam cell story.

Imaging translates these ideas: coronary artery calcium scoring estimates overall plaque burden and refines risk; CT angiography identifies high-risk features (low-attenuation plaque, positive remodeling, napkin-ring sign); intravascular ultrasound and optical coherence tomography measure cap thickness. Regression of atheroma volume with intensive lipid lowering has been demonstrated, although clinical benefit relates more to plaque stabilization than to large changes in stenosis.
levels.expert:
Clinically, atherosclerosis is managed as a whole-body risk problem rather than a single blockage.

Primary prevention starts with a calculated 10-year risk (pooled cohort equations, PREVENT, or SCORE2 depending on region) and is refined by risk enhancers: family history of premature disease, chronic kidney disease, inflammatory conditions, lipoprotein(a) elevation, pregnancy-related complications such as preeclampsia, and South Asian ancestry. When the decision is uncertain, a coronary artery calcium score of zero can support deferring statin therapy in some patients, while a high score supports treatment.

In established disease, the targets are aggressive: intensive LDL lowering (statin first, then ezetimibe or PCSK9-directed therapy if goals are not met), blood pressure control, diabetes therapy chosen for cardiovascular benefit (SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists), smoking cessation, antiplatelet therapy, exercise, and cardiac rehabilitation.

Pitfalls:
- Missing familial hypercholesterolemia: very high LDL, tendon xanthomas, or premature disease should trigger cascade screening of relatives.
- Assuming a 'normal' angiogram means no atherosclerosis; non-obstructive plaque still carries risk.
- Stopping statins for vague muscle aches without a structured rechallenge; true intolerance is less common than reported, and the nocebo effect is documented in blinded trials.
- Focusing on the culprit lesion and forgetting carotid, peripheral and renal beds; polyvascular disease carries the highest event rates.

Senior clinicians remember that the stent fixes a narrowing; the pills, exercise and smoking cessation protect the patient from the next plaque rupture somewhere else.

keyPoints: Atherosclerosis = chronic inflammatory buildup of lipid plaques in artery walls
Key steps: endothelial damage → LDL retention/oxidation → foam cells → fibrous cap over necrotic core
Vulnerable plaques have thin caps and large lipid cores; rupture triggers thrombosis
Many culprit plaques are not severely stenotic beforehand
Main modifiable risks: LDL, blood pressure, smoking, diabetes, inactivity

lessons.title: Stable Angina

levels.kid:
Imagine running up a hill. Your legs need more blood, and so does your heart, because it is working harder too.

If the pipes that feed the heart are narrow, enough blood gets through when you rest, but not when you run. The heart muscle gets hungry for oxygen, and it hurts. That chest pain is called angina.

Stable angina is the kind that is predictable. It comes when someone exercises or gets upset, and it goes away after a few minutes of rest. Doctors help with medicines that make the heart's work easier or open the pipes a little, and sometimes they put in a tiny tube called a stent to hold a narrow pipe open.
levels.hs:
**Angina** is chest discomfort caused by the heart muscle not getting enough oxygen (**ischemia**). **Stable angina** happens in a predictable pattern: triggered by exertion, cold, heavy meals, or emotional stress, and relieved within minutes by rest or a nitrate.

The cause is usually a fixed narrowing from atherosclerosis, typically blocking about 70% or more of a coronary artery's diameter. At rest enough blood flows past it; during exertion the heart's demand rises but supply cannot.

Typical symptoms:
- Pressure, tightness or heaviness in the chest, rather than sharp pain.
- May spread to the left arm, jaw, neck or back.
- Breathlessness, sweating or nausea.

Women, older adults and people with diabetes more often have atypical symptoms such as breathlessness or fatigue alone.

Diagnosis uses the story plus tests: an ECG, stress testing (exercise or medication-based, with ECG, echo or nuclear imaging), and CT coronary angiography.

Treatment has two goals: relieve symptoms and prevent heart attacks.
- Symptoms: beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, nitrates.
- Prevention: aspirin, statins, blood pressure control, quitting smoking, exercise.
- Procedures (stents or bypass surgery) for symptoms that persist or high-risk anatomy.
levels.college:
Ischemia results from a mismatch between myocardial oxygen supply and demand. **Demand** is set by heart rate, contractility and wall stress (preload and afterload). **Supply** depends on coronary flow (perfusion pressure, diastolic time, stenosis resistance) and arterial oxygen content.

The **ischemic cascade** describes the order of events: perfusion heterogeneity → metabolic changes → diastolic dysfunction → regional systolic dysfunction (wall motion abnormality) → ECG changes (ST depression) → chest pain. This is why imaging stress tests detect ischemia more sensitively than ECG alone, and why angina is a late sign.

Classification of chest pain: typical angina meets three criteria (substernal discomfort of characteristic quality, provoked by exertion or stress, relieved by rest or nitrate); atypical meets two; non-anginal one or none. The Canadian Cardiovascular Society grades angina from I (only strenuous exertion) to IV (at rest or minimal activity).

Anti-anginal drug mechanisms:
- **Beta-blockers:** lower heart rate and contractility, lengthen diastole. First line in many patients.
- **Calcium channel blockers:** dihydropyridines dilate arterioles (lower afterload) and coronaries; non-dihydropyridines (verapamil, diltiazem) also slow the heart.
- **Nitrates:** release nitric oxide, mainly venodilating to reduce preload and wall stress; also dilate epicardial coronaries. Tolerance develops with continuous exposure, so a nitrate-free interval is used. Combining nitrates with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors can cause dangerous hypotension.
- **Ranolazine:** inhibits the late sodium current, reducing calcium overload.
- **Ivabradine:** blocks the funny current (If) in the SA node, lowering heart rate without affecting contractility.

Revascularization (PCI or CABG) relieves symptoms; in stable disease, trials such as COURAGE and ISCHEMIA showed that an initial invasive strategy did not reduce death or MI compared with optimal medical therapy for most patients, though it improved angina.
levels.phd:
Stable ischemic heart disease is heterogeneous, and a substantial fraction of patients with angina have no obstructive epicardial disease (ANOCA/INOCA: angina or ischemia with non-obstructive coronary arteries), especially women. Mechanisms include **coronary microvascular dysfunction** (impaired vasodilator reserve from endothelial and smooth muscle abnormalities, rarefaction, or extravascular compression) and **vasospasm** of epicardial or microvascular vessels. Invasive coronary function testing measures coronary flow reserve, index of microcirculatory resistance (IMR), and acetylcholine provocation; stratified therapy guided by these results improved angina in the CorMicA trial.

Physiology-guided revascularization rests on fractional flow reserve. FAME showed that FFR-guided PCI reduced events compared with angiography-guided PCI in multivessel disease, and FAME 2 showed benefit of PCI over medical therapy for FFR-positive lesions, driven mainly by reduced urgent revascularization. Non-hyperemic indices (iFR) produce similar outcomes. The ISCHEMIA trial (2020) randomized patients with moderate-to-severe ischemia on stress testing and found no reduction in the primary composite with an initial invasive strategy over a median of about 3 years, although angina-related quality of life improved, and long-term follow-up continues to be analyzed.

The disconnect between ischemia burden and hard outcomes reflects that most MIs arise from rupture of non-flow-limiting plaques; revascularizing a stable stenosis does not treat the many vulnerable plaques elsewhere. Exceptions where revascularization improves survival include significant left main disease and multivessel disease with reduced LV function, particularly with CABG in diabetic patients (FREEDOM).

Ischemic preconditioning, brief ischemic episodes that make myocardium more tolerant of later prolonged ischemia via adenosine, kinase signaling and mitochondrial permeability transition pore inhibition, is robust in experimental models but has not translated into consistent clinical benefit.
levels.expert:
The history does most of the work in chest pain. Clinicians ask: what brings it on, what relieves it, how long it lasts, and whether the pattern is changing. A clear exertional pattern relieved by rest within minutes is stable angina until proven otherwise. A change in pattern, pain at rest, or pain lasting more than about 20 minutes is unstable and belongs in the emergency department.

Testing choice depends on pretest probability and the patient. CT coronary angiography is increasingly first line in many guidelines for lower to intermediate probability because it rules out disease well and reveals non-obstructive plaque that should change preventive therapy. Functional tests (stress echo, perfusion imaging, stress MRI) assess ischemia burden. Patients who can exercise give extra prognostic information from exercise capacity.

Pitfalls:
- Prescribing a nitrate to someone who uses a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor, risking profound hypotension.
- Stopping a beta-blocker abruptly, which can provoke rebound ischemia.
- Using a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker plus a beta-blocker in someone with conduction disease or reduced ejection fraction.
- Dismissing angina in a woman with normal epicardial arteries; consider microvascular dysfunction or vasospasm.
- Forgetting anemia, thyrotoxicosis, tachyarrhythmias or aortic stenosis as demand-side triggers.

The modern conversation with a stable patient is shared decision-making: stents and bypass relieve symptoms and help specific high-risk anatomy, but for most stable patients the life-prolonging work is risk-factor control, antiplatelet therapy, intensive lipid lowering, and exercise. Cardiac rehabilitation is underused and improves outcomes.

keyPoints: Angina = chest discomfort from myocardial ischemia (supply–demand mismatch)
Stable angina is predictable: triggered by exertion or stress, relieved by rest or nitrate
Demand = heart rate, contractility, wall stress; supply = coronary flow and oxygen content
Anti-anginals: beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, nitrates, ranolazine, ivabradine
In stable disease, optimal medical therapy is the foundation; revascularization mainly relieves symptoms except in high-risk anatomy
Never combine nitrates with PDE-5 inhibitors

lessons.title: Acute Coronary Syndromes

levels.kid:
A heart attack happens when one of the heart's feeding pipes gets suddenly blocked by a clot. The part of the heart muscle after the block gets no oxygen. If the block stays, that muscle starts to die.

People having a heart attack often feel a heavy squeezing in the chest. It may spread to the arm or jaw. They may sweat, feel sick, or be very short of breath.

This is an emergency! You call for help right away. Doctors say 'time is muscle': the faster they open the pipe, the more heart they save. They can use a thin tube through a blood vessel to push the clot away and put in a stent, or give medicine that breaks up the clot.
levels.hs:
**Acute coronary syndrome (ACS)** is a sudden reduction in blood flow to the heart, usually because an atherosclerotic plaque ruptures and a clot forms. It includes three conditions:
- **Unstable angina:** ischemic chest pain (new, worsening, or at rest) without heart muscle death; troponin is not raised.
- **NSTEMI (non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction):** heart muscle dies, shown by a rise in **troponin**, but the ECG shows no ST elevation.
- **STEMI (ST-elevation myocardial infarction):** usually a complete blockage of a coronary artery; the ECG shows ST elevation. This needs the artery opened as fast as possible.

Symptoms: crushing chest pressure lasting over about 20 minutes, spreading to the arm, jaw or back, with sweating, nausea and breathlessness. Some people, especially those with diabetes, older adults and women, have milder or unusual symptoms.

Tests: an ECG within 10 minutes of arrival, and blood troponin measured repeatedly.

Treatment:
- Aspirin straight away, plus a second antiplatelet drug and an anticoagulant.
- For STEMI, emergency **PCI** (balloon and stent through a catheter), ideally within about 90 minutes of first medical contact, or clot-busting drugs (**thrombolysis**) if PCI cannot be done fast enough.
- Long-term: statins, beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, quitting smoking, and cardiac rehabilitation.
levels.college:
The **universal definition of myocardial infarction** requires a rise and/or fall of cardiac troponin with at least one value above the 99th percentile upper reference limit, plus evidence of ischemia (symptoms, new ischemic ECG changes, new Q waves, imaging evidence of new loss of viable myocardium or wall motion abnormality, or thrombus on angiography).

MI types: type 1 is atherothrombotic (plaque rupture or erosion); type 2 is supply–demand mismatch without acute atherothrombosis (e.g. severe anemia, tachyarrhythmia, hypotension); types 3–5 cover sudden death and procedure-related infarction. Myocardial injury (troponin rise without ischemia) occurs in sepsis, pulmonary embolism, myocarditis, renal failure and heart failure.

STEMI ECG criteria: new ST elevation at the J point in two contiguous leads above sex- and age-specific thresholds. STEMI equivalents include new left bundle branch block with concordant changes (Sgarbossa criteria), posterior MI (ST depression V1–V3), and de Winter T waves. Evolution: hyperacute T waves → ST elevation → Q waves and T-wave inversion.

Initial management of ACS:
- Antiplatelets: aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor, prasugrel or clopidogrel).
- Anticoagulation: heparin or alternatives.
- Anti-ischemic: nitrates (avoid in RV infarction, hypotension or PDE-5 inhibitor use), beta-blockers if no heart failure or shock.
- Oxygen only if hypoxemic; routine oxygen showed no benefit (DETO2X).
- High-intensity statin early.
- STEMI: primary PCI; fibrinolysis if PCI delay is too long. NSTE-ACS: risk stratification (e.g. GRACE score) determines the timing of invasive angiography.

Complications: arrhythmias (VF early), cardiogenic shock, mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture, ventricular septal or free wall rupture (days 3–5 classically), LV aneurysm and thrombus, and pericarditis, early or late (Dressler syndrome).
levels.phd:
Myocyte necrosis follows the wavefront phenomenon: after coronary occlusion, irreversible injury begins in the subendocardium after roughly 20–40 minutes and spreads toward the epicardium over hours, which is why reperfusion benefit is strongly time-dependent. Reperfusion itself causes injury: calcium overload, reactive oxygen species, opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore, and microvascular obstruction (the no-reflow phenomenon, often from distal embolization, endothelial swelling and leukocyte plugging). Cardiac MRI shows microvascular obstruction and intramyocardial hemorrhage, both of which predict adverse remodeling. Despite strong preclinical data, cardioprotective strategies against reperfusion injury (cyclosporine in CIRCUS, remote ischemic conditioning in CONDI-2/ERIC-PPCI) failed in large trials, a classic translational gap.

High-sensitivity troponin assays changed diagnostic pathways: 0/1-hour or 0/2-hour algorithms combining absolute values and changes allow rapid rule-out with very high negative predictive value, but they also detect chronic myocardial injury, increasing the need to interpret kinetics and clinical context. Sex-specific thresholds have been debated as a way to reduce underdiagnosis in women.

The STEMI/NSTEMI dichotomy is imperfect: about a quarter of NSTEMIs have a totally occluded culprit artery at angiography, often the circumflex, which is electrically silent on the standard 12-lead ECG. This has driven the proposed 'occlusion MI' (OMI) paradigm, which emphasizes recognizing acute occlusion from subtle ECG patterns rather than strict millimetre criteria.

Post-MI remodeling involves infarct expansion, compensatory hypertrophy, neurohormonal activation, and fibrosis; renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and sympathetic blockade attenuate it. MINOCA (MI with non-obstructive coronary arteries) is a working diagnosis requiring further investigation for plaque disruption, spasm, embolism, spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD), takotsubo syndrome or myocarditis.
levels.expert:
In the emergency department, the ACS workflow is built around minutes. The 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes is read immediately by someone who can activate the cath lab. If the first ECG is non-diagnostic and suspicion is high, repeat it every 15–30 minutes and add posterior or right-sided leads.

Key judgments:
- STEMI or occlusion MI: activate the cath lab; door-to-balloon targets drive everything. If transfer delays are long, fibrinolysis followed by transfer is the alternative, provided there are no absolute contraindications (prior hemorrhagic stroke, recent major trauma or surgery, active bleeding, suspected aortic dissection).
- Very high-risk NSTE-ACS (refractory pain, hemodynamic instability, life-threatening arrhythmia, mechanical complication, acute heart failure): immediate angiography.
- Otherwise, early invasive within 24 hours for high-risk features.

Always consider aortic dissection before anticoagulation and fibrinolysis: tearing pain radiating to the back, pulse or blood pressure differential, neurological deficit, a wide mediastinum. Dissection can extend into the right coronary ostium and mimic an inferior STEMI; giving thrombolytics can be fatal.

Pitfalls:
- Dismissing troponin rises in renal failure without looking at the trend.
- Giving nitrates to an inferior STEMI with RV involvement.
- Missing SCAD in a young woman, often peripartum, where stenting is hazardous and conservative care is usually preferred.
- Treating cocaine-associated chest pain like standard ACS without considering vasospasm and the role of benzodiazepines.

After discharge the outcome depends on secondary prevention: dual antiplatelet therapy for a planned duration, high-intensity statin, ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker when indicated, SGLT2 inhibitor or mineralocorticoid antagonist with reduced ejection fraction, smoking cessation, rehabilitation, and echo to plan defibrillator decisions if ejection fraction stays low.

keyPoints: ACS = unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI; usually plaque rupture with thrombus
Troponin rise distinguishes infarction (NSTEMI/STEMI) from unstable angina
STEMI needs immediate reperfusion: primary PCI, or fibrinolysis if PCI is delayed
ECG within 10 minutes; repeat if non-diagnostic
Exclude aortic dissection before anticoagulants or thrombolysis
Mechanical complications (papillary muscle, septal or free wall rupture) peak days 3–5

lessons.title: Heart Failure

levels.kid:
Heart failure does not mean the heart has stopped. It means the heart is too weak or too stiff to pump as well as the body needs.

When the pump cannot keep up, blood and water back up, like a traffic jam. Water can pile up in the lungs, making it hard to breathe, especially when lying down. Water can also pile up in the legs and feet, making them puffy.

People with heart failure often feel tired because their muscles do not get enough blood. Doctors help with medicines that rest the heart, take away extra water, and help it pump better. Eating less salt and staying active in a safe way help too.
levels.hs:
**Heart failure (HF)** is a condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs, or can only do so at high filling pressures.

Two main types, based on the **ejection fraction (EF)**:
- **HF with reduced EF (HFrEF):** the left ventricle is weak and dilated, EF 40% or less. Common causes: heart attacks, long-term high blood pressure, cardiomyopathies.
- **HF with preserved EF (HFpEF):** EF 50% or more, but the ventricle is stiff and does not fill well. Common in older adults with hypertension, obesity and diabetes.

Symptoms come from congestion and low output:
- Breathlessness on exertion, when lying flat (**orthopnea**), or waking up gasping at night (**paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea**).
- Swollen ankles, weight gain from fluid, fatigue.

Signs: raised jugular venous pressure, crackles in the lungs, an S3, leg edema.

Tests: a blood test for **BNP** (released by stretched heart muscle), chest X-ray, ECG, and an **echocardiogram** to measure EF.

Treatment for HFrEF has four pillars proven to help people live longer: an ARNI or ACE inhibitor, a beta-blocker, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and an SGLT2 inhibitor. Diuretics remove excess fluid to relieve symptoms. Lifestyle steps include limiting salt, daily weights, and exercise training.
levels.college:
Heart failure is a clinical syndrome whose pathophysiology is driven by an initial injury followed by maladaptive compensation.

Compensatory mechanisms:
- **Sympathetic activation:** raises heart rate and contractility acutely, but chronically causes myocyte toxicity, arrhythmias and β-receptor downregulation.
- **Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS):** low renal perfusion triggers renin; angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction, sodium retention and fibrosis; aldosterone drives sodium and water retention and myocardial fibrosis.
- **Vasopressin:** water retention and hyponatremia.
- **Natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP):** counter-regulatory, promote natriuresis and vasodilation, but are overwhelmed.
- **Remodeling:** eccentric hypertrophy and dilation in HFrEF; concentric hypertrophy and fibrosis in HFpEF.

Classification: EF categories (HFrEF ≤40%, HF with mildly reduced EF 41–49%, HFpEF ≥50%); NYHA functional classes I–IV by symptoms; ACC/AHA stages A–D from risk to advanced disease.

Left-sided failure causes pulmonary congestion (dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, pleural effusions). Right-sided failure, most often caused by left-sided failure, causes systemic venous congestion (raised JVP, hepatomegaly, ascites, peripheral edema).

Guideline-directed medical therapy for HFrEF:
- ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) or ACE inhibitor/ARB: blocks RAAS; neprilysin inhibition augments natriuretic peptides.
- Evidence-based beta-blockers (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate).
- MRA (spironolactone, eplerenone).
- SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin), beneficial with or without diabetes.
- Loop diuretics for congestion (symptomatic, not shown to reduce mortality).
- Devices: ICD for persistent EF ≤35% for primary prevention of sudden death; cardiac resynchronization therapy for wide QRS (especially left bundle branch block).

In HFpEF, SGLT2 inhibitors reduce hospitalization; management otherwise targets congestion and comorbidities.
levels.phd:
Heart failure is increasingly understood as a systemic disorder. In HFrEF, myocyte-level defects include impaired calcium handling (reduced SERCA2a activity, leaky RyR2 from hyperphosphorylation), altered β-adrenergic signaling (receptor downregulation, increased GRK2), energetic deficit (reduced phosphocreatine/ATP ratio, shift toward glycolysis), titin isoform changes, and loss of myocytes through apoptosis and necrosis. Interstitial fibrosis is driven by angiotensin II, aldosterone and TGF-β signaling. Disease-modifying drugs largely act by blocking neurohormonal maladaptation rather than by boosting contractility; positive inotropes have repeatedly increased mortality in chronic HF trials, a key lesson of the field.

The mechanism of SGLT2 inhibitor benefit remains debated. Candidate explanations include osmotic diuresis and natriuresis with preferential interstitial decongestion, improved myocardial energetics through ketone utilization, reduced sodium-hydrogen exchanger activity, erythropoiesis, reduced intraglomerular pressure and renal protection, and induction of nutrient-deprivation signaling (SIRT1, AMPK, autophagy). The benefits appear rapidly and across EF categories.

HFpEF is phenotypically heterogeneous. A prominent paradigm (Paulus and Tschöpe) proposes that comorbidities such as obesity, diabetes and hypertension produce systemic inflammation and coronary microvascular endothelial dysfunction, reducing nitric oxide–cGMP–protein kinase G signaling in adjacent myocytes, causing hypophosphorylation of titin, increased passive stiffness and hypertrophy. Obesity-related HFpEF has distinct features, including epicardial fat, plasma volume expansion and pericardial restraint, and GLP-1 receptor agonists improved symptoms and function in obese HFpEF (STEP-HFpEF). Cardiac amyloidosis, particularly transthyretin amyloidosis, is an underdiagnosed HFpEF cause with specific therapies (stabilizers such as tafamidis, silencers).

Recovery is possible: reverse remodeling with GDMT or after removing a cause (tachycardia, alcohol, peripartum, myocarditis) produces 'HF with improved EF', but withdrawing therapy can lead to relapse (TRED-HF).
levels.expert:
In the clinic and on the ward, HF is managed as a chronic disease with acute exacerbations.

Acute decompensation is classified by perfusion (warm/cold) and congestion (wet/dry). Most admissions are warm and wet: give intravenous loop diuretics, monitor urine output, electrolytes and renal function, and look for a trigger: ischemia, arrhythmia (especially atrial fibrillation), uncontrolled hypertension, infection, non-adherence to drugs or salt restriction, NSAIDs, or new valve disease. Cold and wet patients may need inotropes or mechanical support and a decision about advanced therapies.

Chronic HFrEF care has shifted toward rapid initiation of all four pillars, often at low intensity first, then up-titration, rather than one drug at a time over months (STRONG-HF supported intensive early titration). Practical skills: managing hyperkalemia and creatinine bumps without abandoning RAAS blockade, recognizing that a modest rise in creatinine on starting these drugs is expected, and timing beta-blocker changes around decompensation.

Pitfalls:
- Missing the cause: every new HFrEF needs an ischemia evaluation and a search for reversible causes (alcohol, tachycardia-mediated, thyroid, myocarditis, infiltrative disease).
- Labeling breathlessness in an obese, hypertensive older adult as deconditioning when it is HFpEF; BNP may be lower than expected in obesity.
- Missing transthyretin amyloid in an older man with HFpEF, carpal tunnel syndrome, low-voltage ECG and thick walls.
- Giving non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers in HFrEF, which worsen outcomes.
- Forgetting the conversation about prognosis and goals of care in stage D.

Good HF programs combine specialist nurses, remote weight and symptom monitoring, cardiac rehab and palliative care input; the evidence shows the system around the patient matters as much as any single drug.

keyPoints: Heart failure = heart cannot meet demand or only at high filling pressures
HFrEF (EF ≤40%) vs HFpEF (EF ≥50%); mildly reduced EF in between
Symptoms: dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, edema, fatigue; signs: raised JVP, crackles, S3
Neurohormonal activation (sympathetic, RAAS) drives progression
HFrEF four pillars: ARNI/ACEi, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor; diuretics for congestion
BNP and echocardiography are key tests

examples.tr: HFrEF with congestion: diuretics plus four-pillar therapy.

lessons.title: Hypertension

levels.kid:
Blood pressure is how hard your blood pushes on the walls of your blood vessels, like water pushing inside a hose.

Some pushing is needed to get blood everywhere. But if the push is too strong all the time, that is called high blood pressure, or hypertension. It usually does not hurt, so people often do not know they have it. That is why doctors check it with a cuff that squeezes your arm.

Over years, too much pressure can hurt the heart, the brain, the kidneys and the eyes. Eating less salt, moving your body, sleeping well and sometimes taking medicine help bring it down.
levels.hs:
**Blood pressure (BP)** is written as two numbers: **systolic** (pressure when the heart squeezes) over **diastolic** (pressure when it relaxes), measured in millimeters of mercury (mmHg).

Under the 2017 American guideline:
- Normal: below 120/80.
- Elevated: 120–129 systolic with diastolic below 80.
- Stage 1 hypertension: 130–139 or 80–89.
- Stage 2 hypertension: 140/90 or higher.
Some other guidelines, such as European ones, use 140/90 as the threshold for hypertension.

Most hypertension (about 90–95%) is **primary (essential)**, with no single cause; it comes from genes, age, salt intake, obesity, inactivity and alcohol. **Secondary** hypertension has a specific cause, such as kidney disease, hormone problems (excess aldosterone), narrowing of the kidney arteries, or sleep apnea.

Hypertension is called a "silent killer" because it usually causes no symptoms while damaging organs:
- Heart: thickening of the left ventricle, heart failure, heart attacks.
- Brain: strokes and dementia.
- Kidneys: chronic kidney disease.
- Eyes: retinopathy.

Treatment starts with lifestyle: less salt, a diet rich in fruits and vegetables (DASH), weight loss, exercise, less alcohol. Main medicine classes: ACE inhibitors or ARBs, calcium channel blockers, and thiazide diuretics.
levels.college:
Blood pressure = cardiac output × systemic vascular resistance, so hypertension reflects increased output, increased resistance, or both; in established primary hypertension, raised resistance usually predominates.

Regulatory systems:
- **Baroreflex:** carotid sinus and aortic arch stretch receptors buffer short-term changes; they reset to higher pressures in chronic hypertension.
- **Kidney pressure-natriuresis:** in health, a rise in pressure increases sodium excretion, returning volume and pressure to normal. In hypertension this curve is shifted, so higher pressure is needed to excrete the daily salt load, Guyton's central idea.
- **RAAS** and the **sympathetic nervous system** raise pressure through vasoconstriction and sodium retention.
- **Endothelium:** nitric oxide versus endothelin balance.

Measurement matters: proper cuff size, seated rest, arm at heart level, repeated readings, and out-of-office confirmation with home or ambulatory monitoring to detect **white-coat** hypertension (high in clinic only) and **masked** hypertension (normal in clinic, high outside).

Clues to secondary causes: onset at a young age, sudden worsening, resistant hypertension (uncontrolled on three drugs including a diuretic), hypokalemia (primary aldosteronism), episodic headaches, sweating and palpitations (pheochromocytoma), an abdominal bruit or a sharp creatinine rise on ACE inhibitors (renal artery stenosis), snoring with daytime sleepiness (sleep apnea), or arm–leg BP difference in a young person (coarctation of the aorta). Primary aldosteronism is more common than once thought.

Drug choice: ACE inhibitors or ARBs (especially with diabetes, proteinuric kidney disease or HFrEF), dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, and thiazide-like diuretics. Most patients need two or more drugs; single-pill combinations improve adherence. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy.

A **hypertensive emergency** is severe hypertension with acute organ damage (encephalopathy, stroke, MI, acute heart failure, aortic dissection, acute kidney injury, eclampsia).
levels.phd:
Primary hypertension is polygenic: genome-wide association studies have identified more than a thousand loci, each with tiny effects, pointing to renal sodium handling, vascular tone and the natriuretic peptide system. Rare Mendelian forms illuminate the renal sodium hypothesis: Liddle syndrome (gain-of-function in the epithelial sodium channel), glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism, apparent mineralocorticoid excess (11β-HSD2 deficiency), and Gordon syndrome (WNK kinase mutations increasing NCC activity, treated by thiazides). Each raises pressure through increased renal sodium reabsorption, supporting Guyton's model that the kidney sets long-term pressure.

The Guyton model has been challenged by data showing a role for the nervous system, vascular dysfunction, and immune cells. T cells and macrophages infiltrate kidney and perivascular fat in experimental hypertension; mice lacking lymphocytes (RAG1-knockout) have blunted angiotensin II–induced hypertension. Interstitial sodium storage in skin, bound to glycosaminoglycans and regulated by macrophage VEGF-C signaling, adds a non-osmotic buffer to the classical two-compartment model.

Arterial stiffness both results from and contributes to hypertension. Increased pulse-wave velocity and early wave reflection augment central systolic pressure, explaining the rising prevalence of isolated systolic hypertension with age. Central aortic pressure can differ from brachial pressure, which may partly explain why drugs with similar brachial effects had different outcomes in some trials.

Treatment targets have been shaped by trials. SPRINT (2015) found that a systolic target below 120 reduced cardiovascular events and death compared with below 140 in high-risk non-diabetic adults, using standardized unattended measurement, at the cost of more hypotension, syncope and kidney injury. Renal denervation, catheter-based ablation of renal sympathetic nerves, showed modest blood pressure lowering in sham-controlled trials and has regulatory approval in some regions, though its place in practice remains debated.
levels.expert:
Experienced clinicians start by confirming the diagnosis: many 'resistant' patients have white-coat effect, poor measurement technique, or non-adherence. Home BP monitoring with a validated device and a structured protocol is cheap and changes management.

Assessment of a new hypertensive patient: cardiovascular risk calculation, kidney function and urine albumin, potassium, glucose and lipids, ECG for LV hypertrophy, and a targeted screen for secondary causes. Screening for primary aldosteronism with an aldosterone–renin ratio is recommended in resistant hypertension, hypokalemia, adrenal incidentaloma, sleep apnea, or atrial fibrillation without another explanation; it is widely underused, and its unilateral form can be cured surgically.

Resistant hypertension: after excluding pseudo-resistance, optimize a thiazide-like diuretic, then add a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone was most effective in PATHWAY-2).

Severe BP without acute organ damage (hypertensive urgency) is usually managed with oral therapy and early follow-up; rapid lowering can cause stroke or myocardial ischemia because autoregulation has shifted. True emergencies need controlled intravenous lowering in a monitored setting, with targets specific to the condition: aortic dissection requires rapid heart-rate and pressure control, while acute ischemic stroke is usually treated more permissively unless thrombolysis is planned.

Pitfalls:
- Starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB in someone who may become pregnant without counseling.
- Combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB (more kidney injury and hyperkalemia without benefit).
- Ignoring orthostatic hypotension in older patients when intensifying therapy.
- Missing NSAIDs, decongestants or stimulant medications as reversible contributors.

Hypertension is the leading modifiable risk factor for death worldwide; a good doctor treats it persistently, because the benefit accrues silently over years.
